title: Nuclear Medicine: Functional Imaging for the Right Question
bottomLine: Nuclear medicine answers functional/physiologic questions that anatomy alone may not answer. Choose the study only when the indication fits the tracer and the result can change management; pregnancy, breastfeeding, renal function and recent competing imaging/therapy can change timing and interpretation.
recognize: Common applications include bone, thyroid, renal, myocardial perfusion, hepatobiliary and selected oncologic imaging.
Tracer uptake is not synonymous with malignancy; inflammation, healing and benign physiology can also alter uptake.
differentiate: PET/SPECT functional information complements rather than universally replaces CT/MRI anatomy.
A positive scan must be interpreted against pretest probability and the specific tracer's known false-positive patterns.
assessment: Clarify the clinical question, pregnancy/breastfeeding, renal status, recent nuclear medicine tests, medications and recent therapy that may affect uptake.
workup: Use CAR referral guidance and nuclear-medicine protocol to select the correct test and preparation.
Do not repeat a recent adequate study simply because a different service requested it unless a new question exists.
management: Act on results in the disease-specific pathway and seek radiology/nuclear-medicine consultation when uptake is indeterminate or discordant with the clinical picture.
medicationSafety: Radiopharmaceutical exposure requires pregnancy/lactation and radiation-safety review; some studies require medication or dietary preparation according to protocol.
redFlags: Pregnancy with nonurgent radionuclide study
Unexpected high-risk finding requiring urgent specialty action
Severe allergic/reaction history to adjunctive pharmacologic stress agents
counselling: Explain that nuclear medicine shows function/uptake rather than a simple photograph and that abnormal uptake may still need confirmatory evaluation.
followUp: Own incidental or indeterminate findings and ensure recommended anatomic/biopsy correlation is completed.
examTrap: Treating tracer uptake as pathognomonic cancer without considering the indication, tracer and benign/inflammatory alternatives.
oneLinePearl: Nuclear medicine answers a physiology question; the tracer and pretest probability define what the image means.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists Referral Guidelines

title: Screening Tests: Prevalence Changes What a Positive Result Means
bottomLine: Screening applies to asymptomatic populations and changes probability; it does not establish a diagnosis. Interpret a result using disease prevalence, test performance and the downstream confirmatory pathway, and never substitute a screening algorithm for diagnostic evaluation of symptoms.
recognize: Positive predictive value falls when disease prevalence is low even if sensitivity/specificity are good.
False positives create additional testing, anxiety and sometimes procedural harm; false negatives can create false reassurance.
differentiate: A screening mammogram/FOBT/HPV test is not the correct pathway for a new breast mass, GI bleeding or symptomatic cervical disease.
Population recommendations can differ from individualized testing in hereditary/high-risk groups.
assessment: Confirm absence of symptoms, eligibility criteria, family/genetic risk, prior abnormal screens and whether the patient can complete follow-up after an abnormal result.
workup: Use current Canadian/provincial program guidance and the appropriate confirmatory diagnostic test after an abnormal screen.
management: Use shared decision-making when benefit/harm balance is preference sensitive and close the loop on every abnormal result.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary premedication, biopsy or invasive testing before the screening result actually meets diagnostic criteria.
redFlags: Symptoms that require diagnostic rather than screening workup
Abnormal screen without follow-up ownership
High-risk hereditary features outside average-risk screening pathways
counselling: Explain that a positive screen means 'more evaluation needed,' not 'you have the disease.'
followUp: Track abnormal results to definitive resolution and reset future screening intervals based on the diagnostic outcome.
examTrap: Using an average-risk screening test as the workup for a symptomatic patient.
oneLinePearl: Screening estimates risk; diagnosis proves or excludes disease.
sourceBasis: Canadian preventive-health and provincial screening-program guidance
Canadian Association of Radiologists cancer referral guidance

title: Sensitivity and Specificity: Test Performance Changes With the Clinical Context
bottomLine: Sensitivity and specificity describe test performance against a reference standard, while predictive values depend on prevalence/pretest probability. Choose a test based on whether the clinical task is ruling out, ruling in, confirming, staging or monitoring—not because one statistic sounds impressive.
recognize: Highly sensitive tests reduce false negatives when used in the correct population; highly specific tests reduce false positives.
Likelihood ratios are useful for moving pretest probability to post-test probability when they are validated for the setting.
differentiate: Sensitivity/specificity are not the same as PPV/NPV.
A negative result from a sensitive test does not rule out disease if the patient falls outside the validation population or pretest probability is extreme.
assessment: Estimate pretest probability before ordering the test and ask how a positive or negative result will change management.
workup: Use validated clinical decision rules and test characteristics for the population being assessed rather than memorized values detached from setting.
management: If neither result would change the plan, do not order the test.
Escalate to definitive/confirmatory testing when the consequence of a false negative or false positive is high.
medicationSafety: Do not start high-risk treatment from a low-specificity screening result when confirmatory testing is available and clinically appropriate.
redFlags: High-stakes disease with discordant negative test and high clinical probability
Result interpreted outside validated population
Critical treatment decision based on screening-only evidence
counselling: Explain uncertainty using absolute probabilities rather than 'the test is 95% accurate.'
followUp: Reassess when disease probability changes over time or new symptoms emerge despite prior negative testing.
examTrap: Calling a positive result definitive because the test is highly sensitive, or assuming NPV is fixed across populations.
oneLinePearl: Test performance is only useful when it moves probability enough to change care.

title: Point-of-Care Testing: Fast Result, Same Need for Quality and Clinical Correlation
bottomLine: Point-of-care testing shortens time to information but does not remove pre-analytic, analytic or interpretation error. Use a validated device for a defined clinical question, understand when confirmatory laboratory testing is required, and never let a surprising POC result override the patient without verification.
recognize: Glucose, urine tests, pregnancy testing, infectious antigen/molecular assays, INR and selected blood-gas/chemistry platforms are common POC applications.
Operator technique, storage, calibration/quality-control failure and interfering substances can distort results.
differentiate: A POC screening test may need central-laboratory confirmation before a definitive diagnosis or long-term treatment decision.
Turnaround speed does not equal greater diagnostic accuracy.
assessment: Check whether the result fits symptoms/vitals and whether collection/device limitations could explain discordance.
workup: Repeat or send confirmatory testing when the result is unexpected, outside the device's reportable range or clinically high stakes.
management: Use POC results immediately when validated for the acute decision, while documenting/communicating confirmatory plans when needed.
medicationSafety: Do not make major insulin/anticoagulant/antimicrobial changes from an implausible device result without verification when time permits.
redFlags: POC value incompatible with patient condition
Critical result outside device range
Quality-control failure
High-stakes diagnosis without required confirmation
counselling: Explain when a rapid result is preliminary and why another specimen may still be needed.
followUp: Ensure confirmatory results are reconciled with any treatment already started.
examTrap: Assuming a bedside device cannot be wrong because the result is available quickly.
oneLinePearl: POC testing shortens time, not the quality-assurance process.

title: Microbiology Results: Infection, Colonization, Contamination, or Past Exposure?
bottomLine: A positive microbiology result does not automatically equal active infection. Interpret specimen quality, anatomic site, organism, burden, symptoms, host risk and timing; distinguish colonization/contamination from disease and know when molecular/serologic results represent current versus past infection.
recognize: Poor-quality sputum, contaminated urine/blood culture, colonized wounds and asymptomatic bacteriuria can generate positive results without a treatable infection.
NAAT detects nucleic acid and may remain positive after viable organisms fall depending on pathogen/test; serology often reflects immune response rather than direct organism detection.
differentiate: Culture provides viable-organism and susceptibility information but can be slower; NAAT can be faster/sensitive but may not provide full susceptibility data.
A single likely contaminant blood culture differs from persistent growth of a pathogenic organism in a compatible syndrome.
assessment: Start with infection syndrome, severity, immune status, prior antibiotics and specimen collection quality.
workup: Repeat or obtain better specimens when contamination is likely and susceptibility/source-control decisions depend on reliable microbiology.
management: Treat the clinical infection using current Canadian/local guidance and de-escalate or stop therapy when results show colonization or an alternative diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Avoid broadening antibiotics from a colonizing organism without evidence of infection; review allergies, renal function and drug interactions when targeted therapy is needed.
redFlags: Positive blood/CSF culture in compatible severe illness
Persistent bacteremia
Neutropenic infection
High-consequence communicable disease requiring public-health action
counselling: Explain why 'a bacteria grew' does not always mean antibiotics are needed.
followUp: Close the loop on pending cultures/susceptibilities and revise empiric therapy when results return.
examTrap: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria or a colonized wound because the culture report lists an organism and susceptibilities.
oneLinePearl: Microbiology identifies organisms; the syndrome determines whether they are causing disease.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada microbiology/antibiotic stewardship recommendations

title: Immunology Tests: Order for a Phenotype, Not for Vague Symptoms
bottomLine: Autoantibodies and immune tests perform best when the patient already has a compatible phenotype. Low-pretest-probability screening creates incidental positives; order the narrowest test set that answers the differential and interpret titre/pattern plus clinical features rather than diagnosing autoimmune disease from one antibody.
recognize: ANA can be positive in healthy people; disease-specific antibodies are useful only in the right clinical syndrome.
Complement, inflammatory markers and immunoglobulins answer different immune questions and should not be ordered as one universal 'autoimmune panel.'
differentiate: Screening autoantibody positivity differs from disease-defining clinical criteria.
Immunodeficiency testing focuses on recurrent/unusual infection phenotype and quantitative/functional immune assessment rather than autoimmune serology.
assessment: Define organ pattern, inflammatory features, family history, infection history, medications and duration before testing.
workup: Use stepwise disease-specific testing guided by rheumatology/immunology criteria; avoid repeat ANA or broad antibody panels when no new clinical question exists.
management: Refer when the phenotype plus testing suggests systemic autoimmune disease, immune deficiency or organ-threatening inflammation; do not start immunosuppression from a laboratory result alone.
medicationSafety: Before immunosuppression, exclude infection and complete therapy-specific screening/vaccination where indicated.
redFlags: Rapid renal/pulmonary/neurologic inflammatory syndrome
Severe recurrent opportunistic infection
Vasculitic organ ischemia
Pregnancy with disease-specific antibody risk requiring specialty care
counselling: Explain that a positive antibody can be a clue rather than a diagnosis and may occur in healthy people.
followUp: Repeat immune testing only when validated for disease activity or when the clinical syndrome changes.
examTrap: Diagnosing lupus from an isolated positive ANA in a patient with nonspecific fatigue and no compatible clinical features.
oneLinePearl: Immunology tests work best after the phenotype has earned them.

title: Genetic Testing: Start With the Phenotype and Family History, Plan for the Result
bottomLine: Genetic testing should answer a defined clinical/familial question. Build a three-generation family history, choose the appropriate person/test, obtain informed consent for benefits/limitations/secondary findings, and never treat a variant of uncertain significance as pathogenic.
recognize: Red flags include early-onset disease, multiple related cancers, unusual combinations of disease, bilateral/multifocal disease, consanguinity or multiple affected relatives.
Testing an affected relative first often provides more information than starting with an unaffected person when hereditary disease is suspected.
differentiate: Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants differ from VUS and benign/likely benign classifications.
A negative result can be truly reassuring, uninformative or limited by the test's scope depending on the family/phenotype.
assessment: Document personal/family diagnosis and age at onset, ancestry, reproductive implications, insurance/privacy concerns and what decision the result will change.
workup: Use current Canadian testing/referral criteria and appropriate molecular/cytogenetic testing; involve genetics when panel selection or interpretation is complex.
management: Use pathogenic/likely pathogenic findings to guide surveillance, treatment or cascade testing according to current disease-specific guidance.
Do not change major management solely because of a VUS.
medicationSafety: Pharmacogenomic results apply only to validated drug-gene relationships and do not replace standard clinical monitoring.
redFlags: Result with major cancer/cardiac implications and no counselling plan
VUS being used as disease proof
Incidental/secondary finding requiring urgent specialty follow-up
counselling: Discuss possible results before testing and explain that results can affect biologic relatives as well as the patient.
followUp: Revisit variant classification or family history when new evidence or diagnoses emerge.
examTrap: Treating a VUS as a confirmed pathogenic mutation and screening the whole family based on it.
oneLinePearl: Genetic testing is most useful when you know the question and know what you will do with each possible answer.
sourceBasis: Genetics Education Canada — Knowledge Organization (GECKO) clinician resources

title: Tumor Markers: Monitoring Tool or Diagnostic Trap?
bottomLine: Most serum tumor markers are not general cancer-screening tests. Use them only in validated contexts—such as selected diagnosis support, prognosis or treatment/recurrence monitoring—and interpret trends with disease burden, organ function and imaging rather than treating a single elevation as proof of malignancy.
recognize: CA-125, CEA, CA19-9, AFP, PSA and other markers have disease-specific roles and important benign causes of elevation.
Marker kinetics during treatment can be useful only when the marker is relevant to that cancer and interpreted with clinical/imaging response.
differentiate: An elevated tumor marker in an asymptomatic low-risk person is not a cancer diagnosis.
A normal marker does not exclude malignancy when the cancer does not reliably secrete that marker.
assessment: Clarify known/suspected cancer, symptoms, smoking/inflammation, liver/renal disease and whether a baseline marker was previously elevated.
workup: Use disease-specific imaging/pathology for diagnosis; order markers only when current oncology guidance shows the result will change management.
management: Refer suspicious clinical/imaging findings through the appropriate cancer pathway and use marker trends as adjunctive evidence when validated.
medicationSafety: Do not start or change systemic cancer treatment based solely on a nonspecific marker change without confirming clinical/radiographic context.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cancer symptoms despite reassuring marker
Marked marker rise with corresponding clinical deterioration
Abnormal screening-style marker with no diagnostic follow-up plan
counselling: Explain that many tumor markers can be elevated for noncancer reasons and are often more useful after a cancer diagnosis than before one.
followUp: Trend only when the marker has a validated role and use the same assay/context when possible.
examTrap: Ordering a panel of tumor markers to screen an asymptomatic patient for occult cancer.
oneLinePearl: Tumor markers usually monitor a known pathway better than they discover an unknown cancer.
sourceBasis: Canadian oncology and Choosing Wisely Canada recommendations
Canadian Association of Radiologists cancer diagnostic referral guidance
